note: A 44-play subject and sourcing plan, not a finished or rights-cleared image collection. Proposed subjects follow the local registry arguments. Unique illustrations may serve where direct depictions cannot be found. Do not invent ancient evidence.
preferred_direction: Confirmed by owner: distinct drawings based on ancient objects.

plays.author: euripides
plays.title: Medea
plays.proposed_subject: Medea in a dragon-drawn chariot; use the Cleveland vase as a verified source, with a spoiler-aware crop.
plays.status: Drawn in the phase 1 test, 2026-10-02: usable
plays.credit: After the Lucanian red-figure calyx-krater near the Policoro Painter, c. 400 BCE, Cleveland Museum of Art 1991.1, Leonard C. Hanna Jr. Fund; drawn from the museum's detail photograph.
plays.license: CC0 (Cleveland Open Access record: share_license_status CC0, checked 2026-10-02)
plays.crop: Medea in the serpent chariot, cut out of the sun disk along the disk's own border. Left out: the Furies, Jason, the nurse, the tutor and the children's bodies on the altar below. Her right sleeve is outlined by hand: its dark net pattern drops out of the automatic mask and left her hand floating.
plays.alt_text: Medea in a chariot drawn by two serpents
plays.shows: The play itself: the museum ties the scene to Euripides' Medea. It shows the ending (her escape); the dead children are left out.
plays.method: Red-figure photo: clay found by brightness, the disk border cut away per degree around its centre, silhouette edge plus relief lines (black top-hat), house line weight, potrace. tools/medea.py.
plays.result: Usable. Busier than the others: the serpents' painted spots come through as speckle.

plays.author: euripides
plays.title: Iphigenia at Aulis
plays.proposed_subject: A scene from the Met narrative bowl; select the arrival or letter scene after inspecting all views.
plays.status: Failed in the phase 1 test, 2026-10-02
plays.credit: Met 31.11.2, terracotta Megarian bowl, Greek, Boeotian, 2nd century BCE (Purchase, 1931).
plays.crop: Tried: the letter scene in view LC-31_11_2b (the old servant holding out Agamemnon's letter; Menelaus, with his staff, reaching for it). Test file: docs/redesign/drawings/rejected/iphigenia-at-aulis.svg, not for use.
plays.shows: The play itself: the Met record describes five scenes from Euripides' Iphigenia at Aulis, with name inscriptions.
plays.method: XDoG, Canny at three scales and local-contrast thresholds found no usable lines in the worn low relief. A hand outline on a local-contrast copy gave featureless silhouettes. tools/iphigenia.py.
plays.result: Failed. The relief is too low and worn to trace from these photographs, and the Met lists no publication before 1933, so no old drawing is likely. Needs new raking-light photographs, a scholarly drawing whose licence allows reuse, or an original drawing from checked references. The second bowl of the series (ending with Iphigenia and Achilles) is a lead to check.

playwrights.author: aeschylus
playwrights.title: Aeschylus
playwrights.status: Drawn in the phase 1 test, 2026-10-02: clean
playwrights.credit: After Carl Bötticher's drawing of an Apulian red-figure krater by the Black Fury Painter (Naples, Museo Archeologico Nazionale): Orestes at Delphi. C. Bötticher, Der Omphalos des Zeus zu Delphi (Berlin, 1859), plate, fig. 1. Scan: Heidelberg University Library.
playwrights.license: Public domain (published 1859). Heidelberg labels the scan with the Public Domain Mark 1.0 (IIIF manifest, checked 2026-10-02).
playwrights.crop: The Pythia only, cut along her own lines. Left out: Apollo's black cloak, leg and boot beside her, the laver behind her, the black Fury above. Apollo's raised back foot lies across her hem: its lines are erased and the hem is left blank there, with nothing drawn in.
playwrights.alt_text: The Pythia, Apollo's priestess, fleeing in terror with her hands raised
playwrights.shows: Related to the play: Orestes at Delphi, the setting of the Eumenides' opening, where the Pythia comes out of the temple in terror (34 ff.). A painting of the myth, not a record of a performance.
playwrights.method: Engraved plate: ink by threshold with the paper tone divided out; cut by a least-cost path through hand-placed points; house line weight; potrace. tools/pythia.py.
playwrights.result: Clean. The Commons copy of this plate is a blurred 1.5x upscale of the same scan and traced badly; use the Heidelberg file.

playwrights.author: sophocles
playwrights.title: Sophocles
playwrights.status: Drawn in the phase 1 test, 2026-10-02: usable
playwrights.credit: After the Attic red-figure pelike by the Achilles Painter, c. 450/445-440 BCE, Berlin, Antikensammlung F 2355 (ARV² 990.49). Photograph: Gary Todd.
playwrights.crop: Oedipus only; the Sphinx on her rock is a separate figure and is left out. His feet and spear butt are cut along the top of the meander band they stand on. His hair, glaze-dark like the ground, is outlined by hand from the photo.
playwrights.alt_text: Oedipus, a young traveller in cloak and short tunic, standing with a spear
playwrights.shows: Related subject: Oedipus before the Sphinx, the myth before Oedipus Tyrannus begins.
playwrights.method: Red-figure photo: clay found by colour (red minus blue), because the shiny glaze is as bright as the clay; silhouette edge plus relief lines; hair outlined by hand; house line weight; potrace. tools/oedipus_berlin.py.
playwrights.result: Usable. The lower cloak edge is ragged where the vase is restored, and his hand on the spear is rough. Alternate: a public-domain 2009 vector redrawing of Vatican 16541 (seated Oedipus with the Sphinx) traced cleanly (docs/redesign/drawings/alternates/), but it is a modern redrawing, neither an old plate nor a photograph.

playwrights.author: euripides
playwrights.title: Euripides
playwrights.proposed_subject: A directly sourced scene from a surviving play
playwrights.status: Drawn in the phase 1 test, 2026-10-02: clean
playwrights.credit: After R. Jaene's lithograph of the Duke of Buckingham's vase, Archäologische Zeitung 7 (1849), Denkmäler und Forschungen, Taf. XII ('Iphigenia in Tauris'). Scan: Internet Archive.
playwrights.license: Public domain (published 1849). The Internet Archive item page carries no rights statement.
playwrights.crop: Iphigenia with the temple key, its chain and knob. Left out: Pylades, the temple door and steps behind her, Artemis' foot, the attendant's tray. The tablet she and Pylades both hold is cut at its middle: the scan is too coarse to show where her fingers end and his begin.
playwrights.alt_text: Iphigenia, priestess of Artemis, holding out a letter tablet and the temple key
playwrights.shows: The play itself, as the 1849 publication identifies it: Iphigenia giving her letter to Pylades (Iphigenia in Tauris 727 ff.). The vase's present location was not checked.
playwrights.method: Lithograph: fine grey lines found by local contrast (black top-hat; one global threshold broke them up); least-cost cut; house line weight; potrace. tools/iphigenia_tauris.py.
playwrights.result: Clean. Face and dress patterns survive; she is about 750px tall in the scan. Phase 2: give Iphigenia in Tauris itself a different scene.

playwrights.author: aristophanes
playwrights.title: Aristophanes
playwrights.proposed_subject: A comic actor or checked comedy reference
playwrights.status: Drawn in the phase 1 test, 2026-10-02: clean
playwrights.credit: After the Apulian red-figure bell-krater by the Schiller Painter, ca. 370 BCE, Würzburg, Martin von Wagner Museum H 5697 (RVAp 4/4a). Photograph: ArchaiOptix, CC BY-SA 4.0. Drawing traced from the photograph and changed.
playwrights.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (photo by ArchaiOptix, checked 2026-10-02). The drawing is a derivative and is released under CC BY-SA 4.0 with this credit. The file page adds that some museums allow photography for non-commercial use only; that is a note, not a licence term.
playwrights.crop: Mika only. The blade of Mnesilochus' knife, which touches her bowl's rim, is cut away along the blade's edge; Mnesilochus, on the altar, is left out.
playwrights.alt_text: Mika, in a comic old woman's mask, holding out a bowl
playwrights.shows: The play itself, as the vase is read: the mock sacrifice of the wineskin 'baby' in Women at the Thesmophoria, staged as a phlyax play. Mika asks for a bowl to catch its blood at 754-755 (the repo's Hall-Geldart text, where she is the First Woman, called Mikka at 760).
playwrights.method: Red-figure photo: clay found by brightness; silhouette edge plus relief lines; knife cut; house line weight; potrace. tools/mika.py.
